Rhinolophidae.foragingNote: Long CF tone with terminal FM sweep; Doppler-shift compensation; clutter-tolerant, close-space foragers.

Rhinonycteridae.foragingNote: Trident bats, split from Hipposideridae; same high-duty-cycle CF-FM strategy as Rhinolophidae/Hipposideridae.

Rhinopomatidae.foragingNote: Mouse-tailed bats; distinctive very long-duration, narrowband CF pulses with long silent intervals between them (low duty cycle despite CF design).

Cistugidae.foragingNote: Hairy bats (Cistugo), split from Vespertilionidae; broadband FM calls typical of vesper-bat-style edge/clutter foraging.

Hipposideridae.foragingNote: Convergent with Rhinolophidae; CF-FM high-duty-cycle calls for clutter-tolerant foraging.

Mormoopidae.foragingNote: Pteronotus parnellii independently evolved high-duty-cycle CF-FM, convergent with Old World Rhinolophidae/Hipposideridae.

Vespertilionidae.foragingNote: Largest bat family; broadband FM sweeps for precise ranging in open-to-edge space; specific genera vary widely (see examples).

Pipistrellus pipistrellus.foragingNote: Peak ~45kHz; edge-space forager, gave rise to '45kHz pipistrelle' vs '55kHz' (P. pygmaeus) species split.

Nyctalus noctula.foragingNote: Open-air, high-altitude forager; low frequency for long range.

Plecotus auritus.foragingNote: Very low intensity ('whispering bat'); large ears, gleans prey using passive hearing too.

Miniopteridae.foragingNote: Fast open/edge-space foragers, steep FM sweeps.

Molossidae.foragingNote: Open-air, high-altitude, fast-flying foragers; narrowband low-frequency calls for long detection range.

Emballonuridae.foragingNote: Sheath-tailed bats; edge/open-space foragers with narrowband multiharmonic calls.

Noctilionidae.foragingNote: Trawls water surface for fish/insects using CF component to detect ripples.

Phyllostomidae.foragingNote: New World leaf-nosed bats; short, steep, low-intensity multiharmonic FM calls ('whispering'); many are frugivores/nectarivores relying more on vision/olfaction.

Megadermatidae.foragingNote: False vampire bats; low-intensity calls, many glean prey using passive listening as primary sense.

Nycteridae.foragingNote: Slit-faced bats; low-intensity narrowband calls emitted through nostrils; gleaning specialists.

Craseonycteridae.foragingNote: Kitti's hog-nosed bat (bumblebee bat), smallest bat; high-frequency calls suited to fine-scale clutter.

Natalidae.foragingNote: Funnel-eared bats; very high-frequency, short-range calls for slow, maneuverable flight in clutter.

Furipteridae.foragingNote: Smoky bats; limited data, broadband FM typical of clutter foragers.

Thyropteridae.foragingNote: Disk-winged bats; roost in rolled leaves, high-frequency short-range FM calls.

Mystacinidae.foragingNote: New Zealand lesser short-tailed bat; unusually terrestrial foraging behavior alongside aerial hawking.

Myzopodidae.foragingNote: Sucker-footed bats of Madagascar; high-frequency calls, limited published data.

Pteropodidae.foragingNote: Old World fruit bats/flying foxes; no laryngeal echolocation in most genera (navigate by vision/olfaction). EXCEPTION: Rousettus uses tongue-clicking echolocation (see genus note).

Rousettus aegyptiacus.foragingNote: Non-laryngeal tongue-clicks, broadband, used for coarse cave-navigation, not fine prey capture.
